units.sentence: Public high school students can't use, hold or wear phones or similar devices from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes.
units.evidence_span: no public school student in grades nine through 12 shall be permitted to access personal electronic devices during the school day
units.problem: Stated as an absolute, present-tense rule. P-007 itself adds 'except as otherwise provided in this Code section or required by law', and P-013 lets students use a device their IEP, 504 or medical plan requires. The 30-second version never mentions that exception. The rule applies 'no later than July 1, 2027' (P-007) under an Act effective Dec 31, 2026 (P-019), so the present-tense 'can't' is premature. Equating the 'school day' with first bell to last bell also needs P-005, which is not cited.
units.suggested_fix: Starting no later than July 1, 2027, public high school students can't use, hold or wear phones or similar devices from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes, unless an IEP, 504 or medical plan requires one. [P-007, P-003, P-005, P-002, P-013]

units.sentence: Students in public high schools, their families, and the school staff who enforce the rules.
units.evidence_span: no public school student in grades nine through 12 shall be permitted to access personal electronic devices
units.problem: P-007 covers students and P-014 covers 'designated school personnel', but neither cited passage mentions families or parents.
units.suggested_fix: Add a passage that covers parents, e.g. [P-007, P-011, P-014]. P-011(B) requires parents to contact the school directly.

units.sentence: Schools must start by July 1, 2027, at the latest.
units.evidence_span: Beginning no later than July 1, 2027, no public school student in grades nine through 12 shall be permitted to access personal electronic devices during the school day

units.sentence: Each district sets details like phone storage and how parents reach students.
units.evidence_span: Establish appropriate methods for storing students' personal electronic devices
units.problem: Storage is a local choice (P-009), but the state largely decides how parents reach students. District protocols must send emergency communication through school systems and must 'Require parents or guardians who need to communicate with their student during the school day to contact the school directly' (P-011). So the sentence overstates local discretion. P-008 also puts the duty on 'each local school system and public school', not only on districts.
units.suggested_fix: Each district and public school sets details like phone storage and how families contact the school, within the state rule that parents go through the school. [P-008, P-009, P-011]

units.sentence: That is where families can still have a say.
units.marker: {analysis: the state decision is final; districts adopt and revise their own policies each year under P-008}
units.problem: 'The state decision is final' overstates. The legislature can amend the statute, as HB 1009 amended the 2025 law (P-006, P-007, P-028). No passage describes a public-input process for district policies. And because P-011 already fixes the parent-contact channel, families have little say over how parents reach students. P-008 does support annual adoption and revision 'as appropriate'.
units.suggested_fix: Districts must adopt, and revise as needed, their policies by January 1 each year (P-008), so local school boards are one place families can raise concerns.

framing_issues.text: An Emory epidemiologist said policies can address this with "rapid parent notification systems and guaranteed access to phones when needed."
framing_issues.issue: This sits under 'What the law says', but it is an expert's recommendation, not law. The law as excerpted (P-011) provides neither rapid parent notification nor guaranteed phone access, so readers may think it does. The quote also omits her first sentence, 'Parents' concerns about emergency access are valid and understandable' (P-037), and she is left unnamed while other speakers are named.

framing_issues.text: What supports it: This concern is mainly about safety, trust and priorities, so evidence can't fully settle it.
framing_issues.issue: The opponents' emergency-contact argument gets a 'What supports it' slot with no support, only a reason to discount evidence. Arguments 1 and 2 get study evidence in the same slot. Available support goes unused: Adams's lockdown account (P-049) and P-037's 'valid and understandable'.

framing_issues.text: What supports it: In the English study, students at schools with strict rules used phones about 40 minutes less during school time.
framing_issues.issue: This is listed as support for the mental-health claim, but it measures in-school phone time, not mental health. The same study found no well-being difference (P-042, P-043). It supports only the premise that bans cut in-school phone time.

framing_issues.text: That study measured well-being and phone use, not test scores.
framing_issues.issue: Caveats are uneven. The English study (counter-evidence) gets four limitations (lines 93 and 103), one of which the abstract excerpts cannot verify. The Florida study (supporting evidence) gets timing and working-paper caveats but none on its design: it is quasi-experimental and relies on building-level phone-use data (P-038), and the source hedges the absence result ('the findings suggest', P-040).

Items 2-5 (the bell-to-bell definition, storage rules, emergency-communication protocols and the IEP/504 exception) are presented as changes, but the passages do not show they are new. The title says the bill revises 'a definition' (P-001), and P-021/P-004 show that this is the device list. P-020 shows the prior law already required district policies 'at a minimum'. These may be existing K-8 rules now extended to grades 9-12.

framing_issues.text: How much focus, learning and well-being will improve in Georgia high schools
framing_issues.issue: This assumes the outcome supporters predict. Given the no-effect well-being findings (P-042, P-043), the neutral wording would be 'whether and how much ... will change'.

framing_issues.text: Whether short phone breaks would cancel out the focus benefits.
framing_issues.issue: This assumes the ban has focus benefits, which the passages do not measure.

framing_issues.text: The day would have less phone-free time.
framing_issues.issue: For the failed amendment, the benefit is hedged ('could', line 80) but the cost is stated as certain ('would'), which tilts the comparison toward the enacted bill.

framing_issues.text: That is where families can still have a say.
framing_issues.issue: This implies the state decision is final (the tag says so outright) and that families can shape how parents reach students, which P-011 already sets at state level. No passage describes a public-input process.

framing_issues.text: This is a disagreement about who should decide and what school is for, not about facts.
framing_issues.issue: Both arguments classed as values questions (3 and 5) are opponents' arguments, and each has empirical parts: teen self-regulation (P-052) and learning responsible use (P-035). Calling argument 5 'not about facts' sets those parts aside.

framing_issues.text: A 2025 law already barred students in kindergarten through 8th grade
framing_issues.issue: 'Public' is dropped here and in lines 45, 64 and 71, though the law covers only public school students (P-006, P-007). Readers could assume private schools are covered.

framing_issues.text: 87.7% of parents who back a ban gave that reason.
framing_issues.issue: Subgroup percentages (87.7%, 69.1%, 74.8%, 45.5%, 41.9%) appear without the overall split (70.8% support vs 29.2% oppose, P-033), so readers cannot tell how many parents overall hold each view.

framing_issues.text: Each district could keep setting its own high school phone rules.
framing_issues.issue: Option A's 'Who benefits' names only districts. It leaves out students and parents who wanted phone access (29.2% of parents opposed a ban, P-033; Adams, P-048), while Option A's 'Who pays' line is framed around students.
